paras: The lynching of Thomas Frazier was the killing of a white man by masked men at Blount's Creek, in Beaufort County, North Carolina, on the night of May 5–6, 1888. Accused of shooting Joshua Cox, a lumberman who had refused him liquor, Frazier was taken from a guarded temporary prison and shot to death where Cox had fallen. Wire reports carried the story nationally, while North Carolina papers disagreed over whether it was justice or a disgrace.

Blount's Creek lay about 16 miles from Washington, North Carolina, where Cox kept a store and a lumber mill. Frazier worked for Cox's brother, H. Mac Cox, and the Tarboro Southerner described him as "a white man." The Washington Gazette reported "bad blood" between Frazier and Cox and called Frazier a "desperate character" who had confessed to several other murders.

On Saturday, May 5, Frazier, who had been drinking, entered Cox's store with two friends, Newton and Adams, and demanded liquor, which Cox refused. As Cox walked toward his mill, Frazier took a gun from one of his friends and fired both barrels of buckshot into him, killing him almost instantly. Frazier fled to H. Mac Cox's house, where his employer and others seized and bound him.

He was chained to a post in a small dwelling near the mill, under sentinels posted by a magistrate, to be taken to the county jail the next morning. According to the Gazette, masked men slipped past the sentinels toward morning, overpowered the guard, knocked off Frazier's irons, and gagged and bound him. They dragged him to the spot where he had fired on Cox and shot him with guns and pistols, "mutilating him almost beyond recognition."

A coroner's inquest on Sunday returned a verdict of death "at the hands of parties unknown to the jury," and a week later the lynchers had still not been found. Frazier's companions, W. B. Adams and John M. Newton, fled armed into the swamps and were outlawed on affidavit as accessories to Cox's murder.

Newton was captured about May 18 and jailed in Washington, where a mob that gathered to lynch him was turned back by guards. A grand jury indicted him for murder in early June, and by December he had been convicted as an accessory after the fact and had appealed to the state Supreme Court. Adams was still in hiding in June.

The story moved first as a Washington, North Carolina, dispatch that appeared on May 7 in Richmond, New Haven, Waterbury and St. Paul. Its headlines treated the lynching as punishment: "A Murder in the South Quickly Punished" in New Haven, "A Murderer Killed by a Mob" in Waterbury, and "Served Him Right" in St. Paul. A shorter version called Frazier "a saloon keeper," sometimes spelled his name Fraser, and was still being reprinted in Kentucky and Dakota in mid-May.

Closer to home, the Washington Gazette headlined "Terrible Murder Speedily Avenged" and praised Cox as "a peaceable and useful citizen." The Raleigh State Chronicle, by contrast, ended its report with the single word "Disgraceful." The Economist, quoted in the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer, saw in the affair both "a diabolical purpose of murder" and "a defiance of law and the constituted tribunals of justice."

The Richmond Dispatch's Raleigh correspondent noted that North Carolina had lynched five people in 1888 without a single legal execution. He later relayed the claim of Beaufort County citizens that corrupt jurors had freed so many murderers that "Judge Lynch is a necessity," tying the case to a lynching of a man named Parker in March. At year's end a Dakota paper's list of "Victims of Judge Lynch" included "Thomas Fraser at Blount's Creek, N. C."

The Gazette and the wire placed Frazier under guard in a dwelling or farm house awaiting the county jail, while the State Chronicle said he was "lodged in jail" and taken from it. The local account is the more detailed and calls the building a "temporary prison."

A 'crowd' or 'company' of masked men overpowered or evaded the guard, took Frazier from custody and shot him to death without any legal process (A1, A2, A8); the papers framed it as avenging his killing of Cox, and a Raleigh letter said Beaufort citizens held 'Judge Lynch' necessary because corrupt juries freed murderers (A8, A11).
The Washington Gazette's local account, the Washington, N.C., wire, the Raleigh State Chronicle and the Tarboro Southerner agree on the killing of Cox and the lynching of Frazier (A2, A8, A10, A12).

The Richmond Dispatch's Raleigh letters counted Frazier among the state's five lynchings of the year and relayed Beaufort citizens' complaint about corrupt jurors.
